So, dear colleagues, can I kindly ask you to take your seats so we can start? Yes. So, dear colleagues, let's start with this event. Thank you for being here. Really important topic. So, thank you for joining this event on Black Sea and global food security in broader sense, where we are showcasing the EU's call for Black Sea grain arrangement. Our Ukrainian friends are joining us. I mean, the minister will be with us soon. They have a bilateral agreement with President Trump, so it takes time. But going to the topic, Russia's war of aggression has consequences that reach beyond Ukraine. Back in 2022, when the prices of agricultural products began to soar worldwide, it became clear to all the strategic importance of the Black Sea for global security, for international trade, for energy and food security. And Ukraine is one of the world's most important important agricultural exporters. It supplies 15% of global maize exports, 10% of wheat, 15 to 20% of barley, and 50, 5-0, percent of global sunflower oil exports. Around 90% of these goods move through the Black Sea corridor, which remains the most important route for Ukrainian grain to reach international markets. Since August, however, exports through Black Sea have effectively grounded to halt. Yet again, Russia's escalating attacks have made commercial shipping unviable. The conflict in the Gulf, combined with the effects of climate change, are also stressing global food production and supply chains. Food must never be used as a weapon. in the Black Sea or anywhere else. Wars make affordable food disappear from dinner tables of millions of people around the globe. But the EU is helping to reduce that impact. In 2025 alone, the EU mobilized 2.1 billion euro to strengthen food security globally through both short-term relief and supporting long-term resilience. In Ukraine, specifically, the EU is helping to alleviate the immediate consequences by identifying grain storage options, keeping farmers and agri-food SMEs afloat who cannot sell this year, and facilitating border crossings for cargo. Since May 2022, the EU solidarity lanes have facilitated trade to the tune of around 304 billion euro. However, the looming global food crisis demands a wider diplomatic Let's look at what has worked in the past. Between 2022 and 2023, the Black Sea Grain Initiative was instrumental in stopping a global food security crisis from happening. I'm glad we are joined today by OCHA, UNOPS, and the World Food Programme. What has been done since then, or what was done then, and what can be also done now? Together, the international community should encourage diplomatic efforts to ensure that there is safe passage of civilian vessels, protect the critical infrastructure, and restore vital global trade routes. And if Russia simply stopped its attacks in the Black Sea, farmers, traders, and international food markets would have the predictability they need at this critical moment. And on top of the Ukrainian calls for a full and unconditional ceasefire since March 2025, the presence of President Zelensky, I hope he can join, or Foreign Minister Zbyh with us today shows that Ukraine has been once again ready to work for the diplomatic solution this so much requires. So as we don't have the Ukrainian representative. So I will first give the floor to my co-chair, Jean-Noel Barrot, the Foreign Minister of France. Please, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Kaja, Madam Vice-President. Ministers, ladies and gentlemen, let me first thank Kaja Kallas for convening this important discussion and pay tribute to all those who keep grain and food going out of Ukraine's ports, often at tremendous personal risk. France stands firmly by the side of Ukraine. For more than four and a half years, Russia's war of aggression has continuously targeted the fields, the barns, the ports, and the ships that feed the world. The relentless attacks are not simply attacks on Ukraine. They constitute a deliberate and cynical strategy to strangle agricultural trade and jeopardize food security across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. Let us be clear about what's at stake. Ukraine has historically supplied between 7 and 10% of the world's grain exports. A prolonged blockade of its deep-sea ports could impose a considerable cost to Ukraine's economy, while the human cost will be paid far beyond Ukraine's borders by the most vulnerable populations. These intensifying attacks come at a time when global food security is already stressed by climate change, with El Nino set to become very strong this year, and by the impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on fertilizers trade. This is why France supports, without any reservation, the call for a moratorium on attacks against civilian vessels, ports, and export infrastructure in the Black Sea. Ukraine put forward such a proposal on the 13th of August. It was cynically rejected by Russia. We regret this refusal and we renew our call on Russia to accept it and to stop weaponizing grain supply. Responding to the immediate consequences of aggression and war is not enough. France is also committed to building global food security and nutrition through resilience activities. In the wake of the conflict in Ukraine, France has made a point of supporting food security in Africa through the Farm Project, a commitment reaffirmed during the Africa Forward Summit that will help increase funding for smallholders farmers. French G7 presidency is putting the protection of grain exports in the Black Sea on top of its agenda. We discussed this matter yesterday evening together with Minister Cebia to mobilize international support. We are also proud to champion, alongside our partners, the School Meals Coalition, which today brings together more than 100 countries, including Ukraine, determined to ensure that every child everywhere can learn with a full stomach. In 2025, we also hosted the Nutrition for Growth Summit in Paris, which secured more than US$30 billion in pledges to fight against malnutrition. Food security in the Black Sea cannot be separated from the quest for peace. We continue to support a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine, one that respects its sovereignty and territorial integrity, that includes an immediate and complete ceasefire starting from the line of contact. Protecting grain shipments is not a substitute for ending this war. It is a first urgent step towards it. The world cannot afford to let hunger become a weapon. France will continue to stand with Ukraine, with the countries most affected by this crisis, and with all those who choose the path of peace over the path of war. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Jean-Noel. And now I give the floor to another co-chair, the Foreign Minister of Romania, Oana Toia, please.

Thank you very much. First of all, thank you, Karakallis, for convening this. And Minister Barrot, it's a very important conversation, looking forward to Minister Cibihad to join us. I'm speaking now on behalf of Romania because we are the country that is facilitating the transit currently for most of the cereals coming out of Ukraine through the port of Constanza in the Black Sea. In the same time, we're also one of the main grain producers inside the European Union. And I mentioned this just to clarify that the risks that we see at the Black Sea are absolutely essential to be tackled, first of all, to allow for the food security we need across the world. And it is great that Ukraine has taken on the leadership on this to propose a very clear solution that we have now on the table. And here at UN throughout this week, we can make it hopefully together a reality. Russia's continuous attacks against Ukraine ports and maritime infrastructure are not only attacks against Ukraine, but they threaten one of the essential channels through which food reaches global markets. And it puts additional pressure on countries and populations already exposed to food insecurity. And in the same time, it increases the price of access to food everywhere, even in countries that do not face the challenge of food insecurity. but that face the pressure of cost of living in general. So in that sense, I think all countries have a mandate, an indirect mandate from their citizens to contribute to a solution. What happens in the Black Sea, therefore, has consequences far beyond the region in Africa, Middle East and Asia. And we have also seen the challenge firsthand. It is often that when a Ukrainian infrastructure is attacked, especially on the Danube or specifically the transit infrastructure, those have become increasingly closer to our border and we have seen more than just in the recent months, more than 100 incursions. One specific case at the border crossing was exactly when the shipments were taking place. And again, I'm speaking about grain shipments, which in absolutely no angle can be seen as a military threat. Since the beginning of Russia's full scale aggression, almost 60 million of Ukrainian grain and agri-food products have transited Romania to the Constanza Harbor and through the Black Sea to the global markets. What we've done in the last year is we've extended capacity on the entire logistical chain, port of Constanza, the lower Danube, a border crossing, and the longer road and rail connections. We have done so in close coordination with Ukraine, Republic of Moldova, actually just A couple of days ago in Chisinau, President Icușor Dan has met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and President Maia Sandu together with us, ministers, specifically to map what are the bottlenecks now and what need to be done. Of course, the European Commission has played a key role throughout this with the EU Solidarity Lanes framework. Now, we have put forward the national investment and sustained efforts, but we do understand this is not enough in terms of the volumes that need to transit and the volumes that need to reach the global markets. And that is why we're strong supporters of the solution put forward today. There's a limit to what alternative routes can achieve, and especially given the high risk of accident, bottlenecks, and pollution. Land and river corridors can mitigate the impact of disruptions, but they cannot replace the Black Sea as the main maritime gateway for grain exports. That's why protecting the freedom of navigation and commercial shipping in the Black Sea is not just a regional concern, it's a global food security imperative. What we are doing at the Black Sea, for example, is together with Bulgaria and Turkey at the NATO Ankara Summit, we have finish the partnership to protect critical infrastructure. But it is essential the work that we're doing with Bulgaria and Turkey inside NATO and, of course, in strong partnership with Ukraine on the demining activities. And that is an ongoing work, as we see an increased number of drifting mines and recently drifting drones in the Black Sea. We also believe it is needed that the operational work for the maritime security hub is into place so that we have that infrastructure in Romania and Bulgaria by end of the year to be able to have a proper and more timely exchange of information with Ukraine as well and other countries at the Black Sea and institutions. From the Black Sea to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, the message is clear. Attacks on vital maritime routes do not remain confined to the waters where they occur. They threaten global food security, energy, and economic stability. To put it simply, in face of the challenges, we're all in the same boat. No infrastructure or national effort can substitute the basic principle of commercial shipping and food export infrastructure must be protected. Since late July, the systematic attacks against Ukrainian ports and vessels operating through these maritime corridors have demonstrated how vulnerable this lifeline remains. A moratorium on attacks affecting food exports could therefore serve as a practical confidence-building measure as well. It is one of the areas where we do also think that all of the countries at the Black Sea and all of us around the table have a direct interest for the moratorium. So it can be one of the fast measures of confidence building that we need for the overall peace conversation going forward. It is complemented, not replacing the broader objective of a full and unconditional ceasefire. We stand ready to continue doing our efforts. And we encourage the UN, European Union, and all our allies and partners to promote this moratorium further. Thank you for your leadership.

Thank you very much. And now I want to give the floor to the agencies who play a key role in food delivery and alleviating the situation in many affected countries caused by the impediment of grain exports from the Black Sea. So first, I will give the floor to you, Tom, please.

Thank you, Kyia, thank you, High Representative, and thank you to the Co-chairs, Excellencies, colleagues. I will select my words more carefully than I usually do because it has been made clear from a number of quarters that we must stick to a purely humanitarian intervention at this stage. So let me offer you that, firstly, the humanitarian perspective. Of course, our position is straightforward. It applies to all parties equally. Civilians and civilian objects must be protected everywhere by everyone. International humanitarian law must be respected by all sides. Safe navigation and the movement of food to global markets must always be safeguarded by all sides, everyone, everywhere. Let me perhaps add a couple of extra points based on my recent visit to Ukraine. We've discussed already yesterday's meeting, the situation with drones. The other big concern during that visit was, of course, the humanitarian situation through the winter, particularly power supplies. And then thirdly, this issue of the situation across the Black Sea. Rania will be able to speak in much more detail about the consequences of the lack of transit of maritime convoys across the Black Sea for countries well beyond the region. So these are countries where when ports, shipping, grain infrastructure is placed at risk, the effects are felt far, far, far beyond the Black Sea, across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. And so people who are playing no part in this war are paying a big consequence for it. So we do need to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea. We need civilian shipping to be able to move safely, ports and infrastructure to be protected, so food can continue reaching global markets. And this very practical objective should not have to wait for wider progress on the political settlement. And as you've said, Kai, we've demonstrated in the past that practical arrangements are possible with the Black Sea Grain Initiative, even in the midst of war, when there is sufficient political will. And the Secretary-General has made clear, including in in meetings that George and I have just been in with the president of Turkey and others that we are ready to work with all parties to support practical arrangements. UNOPS are the experts on the mechanism that could be developed to reduce the risks to civilian shipping and help to restore safe navigation and food exports. If we can do that and reduce those risks and keep food moving safely, then that will be serious and significant and welcome humanitarian progress in its most independent, impartial and neutral spirit. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Tom. And now I want to give the floor to World Food Program, Deputy Executive Director of of. Sorry, Rania Dagash Kamara, please.

Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, thank you for organizing this side event, and thank you, Tom, for your comments, which we fully support. If we can advance solutions that can get more food and agriculture supplies through not only the Black Sea, but also the other two maritime corridors being choked today, then this could be one of the most important conversations at UNGA. Why? Because there's 266 million people today that are acutely hungry across the world, and there's a risk of tens of millions more joining them if the disruptions to maritime trade and the triple choke point continue on for experts on agricultural inputs in the Black Sea, in the Strait of Hormuz, and in Bab el-Mandeb. Because with these choke points and the disruption, supply is down in local markets where we procure. Because commodity prices have shot up and the shock to energy markets have driven higher fuel prices. So what has all that done? Brought higher production costs, more complications to farmers planning the next harvest. Because the poorest households are being priced out of the basics in life. and higher farming costs have put the future harvest in peril. Because we're worried about the long-term risk if shipping lanes remain shut. Because farmers may have far less incentives for the 2027 harvest. Hence, it's in everyone's interest to find solutions so that food and agricultural inputs keep flowing. We are on course for a much larger threat to global food security and wider stability unless urgent action is taken. And hence, humanitarian corridors must remain open and the flow of food and core agricultural commodities must continue safely and predictably. The key now is back with you. It's for member states to prioritize working on the measures to put this into practice and to build the consensus. I do hope that this conversation will be the first step in that direction. And with that, I thank you.

Thank you very much. I also want to acknowledge the presence of Under Secretary General of UNOPS, Jorge Moreira de Silva, being present here because you have been closely involved of this issue through the contacts with different stakeholders. And with that, I also want to give the floor to the International Chamber of Commerce, the Secretary General, John Denton, who has been involved in the creation of the Black Sea Corridor in 2022. So maybe to highlight the lessons learn from there. So over to you.

Thank you very much. And thanks for also including the voice of the private sector in this discussion. The International Chamber of Commerce that I represent, we're in 170 countries. Actually, we're in all your economies. But importantly, we're also in 70% of the ICCs in the global south. And the reason I say that is that recent developments in the Black Sea underscore a fundamental reality. When critical trade routes are disrupted, the consequences are felt far beyond the immediate conflict zone, and we feel it at the ICC through our antenna on the ground immediately. We see and feel the tremors coming. They are felt by a farmer in East Africa waiting for fertilizer, by a family facing rising food prices, and by humanitarian agencies struggling to secure supplies for the world's most vulnerable populations. Let's be clear, the private sector that we represent is deeply concerned by a convergence of food security risks. The blockade of key Black Sea ports, continued disruptions affecting the Strait of Hormuz, and by the way, I proudly work with UN Ops in developing the mechanism that could be deployed to alleviate some of that when the political circumstances arise that may give life to it. and the potential return, obviously, of El Nino conditions. These all threaten to place additional strain on what are already very fragile food systems. The full effects may not be visible today. In fact, they are likely to emerge only in the coming months through reduced harvests, tighter supplies and higher prices. But that is precisely why there is a strong case for early, coordinated, preventive action right now. So in this context, the ICC strongly welcomes the effort to focus attention on the Black Sea. At the International Chamber of Commerce, we have seen the importance of timely action before. We conceived of, actually, Minister, in my office in Paris, the concept note which actually gave birth to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, and I took it to the Secretary-General with a strategy about how it could be delivered. We helped support the development of that and then worked with UNCTAD to deliver it. A very good example, by the way, of something which is rarely seen, which is public-private collaboration in the multilateral space, and frankly, it delivers. We brought the perspective of business operating across agricultural supply chains, shipping networks, and commodity markets. We know what it takes to get the ecosystem, which actually surrounds the economy, which needs to be pushed functioning. This initiative demonstrated what international cooperation can achieve. You know, nearly 33 million tonnes of grain and food products were exported through a humanitarian maritime corridor, helping to stabilise markets. In fact, the announcement of the coordination possible through the Black Sea Grain Initiative immediately dropped food prices by 13 to 15%. We're able to reduce those food prices and support critical humanitarian operations around the world. But perhaps its most important achievement was restoring confidence. It showed that trade can be a powerful humanitarian tool when political cooperation exists. Today, and we are very present, in fact, we keep the private sector functioning in Ukraine. Our network there is sending a clear message. There is an urgent need to get grain moving again before storage capacity, and this is a misunderstood or poorly understood issue. Storage capacity will be reached in the coming six weeks. Delays will have consequences not only for Ukraine, but for global food availability and affordability. ICC therefore stands ready to work with the international partners to ensure that any solution to reopen the Black Sea is commercially and economically workable, operationally practical, and capable of supporting the scale of exports, that's important, the scale of exports required in the months ahead. The lesson from the Black Sea experience is clear. Preventing a food crisis is a hell of a lot easier than responding to one. So the time to act is before the impacts are visible, not after they are felt. Thank you for the opportunity to participate on this, and your recognition that the private sector has a role to play and should play a role in this discussion.

Absolutely, private sector is vital, I mean, working together with organizations and the countries around the table. I'm happy that we have so many foreign ministers present. So let me now give the floor to the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade from Ireland, Helen McEntee, please.

And thank you to our Thank you to our friends and colleagues in Romania and France, and of course Ukraine, for organising today's discussion and again shining a light on what are significant challenges on global food security as a result of Russia's absolutely appalling actions. in the Black Sea. These are, as we've heard, impeding Ukraine's ability to export its grain, its agricultural products freely and safely. They're losing valuable revenues, again, grain that's sitting in silos, unable to be exported, causing significant hardship, not just for its agricultural sector, but at a time when it clearly needs these finances at a very difficult time. It's not merely an issue of concern for Ukraine, and I suppose that's why we're here, and that's why it's so important that we have so many other colleagues here as well. Continued instability in the greater for most, the worsening climate and El Nino-related impacts on agricultural production globally, with disruption to shipping in the Black Sea, has really become such an important contributory factor to what might be a very, very difficult crisis on our doorstep. And of course, we can all see it from an agricultural farming community, the impact it's having on fertilizer, on food prices, and the ability to produce food at a price and a rate that we need it to is significant. But this goes obviously far beyond Europe and will affect the lives and livelihoods of millions and millions of people. It is a solvable problem and I suppose that's why we are here. The key issue is that despite best efforts, there's currently no fully effective alternative to Black Sea shipping grains. So we need to make the Black Sea work. And again, that means effort from everybody in this room. We should be clear that food must never be used as a weapon of war. Valuable or vulnerable people far from the region should not be casualties of Russia's war of aggression with which they have absolutely nothing to do. We should also be clear that the blockages, the impediments and the risks in the Black Sea are entirely man made and as a result of Russia's illegal aggression against Ukraine, the interruption of international shipping and the interface with freedom of navigation is a violation of international law. And so as a collective Our objective should be to exert all of our influence to put a stop to attacks on cargo vessels in the Black Sea. Ukraine must be able to export its agricultural produce. Countries dependent on those supplies should not be made increasingly vulnerable through attacks on maritime trade and infrastructure. Again, due to the attacks by the Russian military operations, global food security is on the brink of a crisis. And so this positive collective action that we are undertaking here today can mitigate against the worst results of such a crisis. So we welcome this renewed effort. We welcome this renewed focus. We will, of course, play our part and do whatever we can. And we will, of course, continue to support Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, the respect for international law, freedom of navigation, and, above all, the protection of their citizens. Thank you.
Thank you. And now I give the floor to Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bulgaria, Velislava Petrova Tziamova.

Thank you, Kaya. And thank you all for the really timely initiative. I will try not to repeat what my colleague said and focus on two parts. First, we really will join the call for a moratorium on attacking the Black Sea and the full unconditional ceasefire there. It's extremely important, as everybody said, not just about the region, but broader food security. I want to outline two initiatives, one of them mentioned by my Romanian colleague about the Black Sea security hub, and really hope that we would manage to keep the momentum and show that this is an initiative that helps not only the countries in the region, but also is an asset to the entire EU. And that's something that is really important for the Black Sea resilience. I also want to highlight a second initiative where Bulgaria will host next year a regional connectivity summit, trying to really put forward the topic of how do we overcome global choke points and how do we ensure that our region can have this alternative routes. You can't have connectivity, you can't have truly, you can't fully use the middle corridor if you don't have safe navigation and shipping through the Black Sea. So that's a prerequisite there. And that's something that it's really important for us too. So I really encourage you to watch forward and participate in those initiatives because it really allows us to bring concrete ideas forward and to really ensure that we have food security that all of our citizens deserve. Thank.
You. Thank you. And now I give the floor to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Hungary, Jani Torvan, please.

Thank you, dear Kaja, Jean-Noel, Oana, for organizing this very important meeting and also bringing global attention to the dire situation in the Black Sea region that affects countries near and far and bring to the global food situation to our attention and agenda. Since the beginning of Russia's war against Ukraine, security in the Black Sea region has become a regular issue of discussion, and I believe it's timely that we also discuss it at the UN setting here in New York. Our common efforts must bring and enforce stability and resilience of all states of the region, and this is important not only for the region, but for the global food security as well. Russia's attacks against Ukraine's ports, ships, and grain facilities are unacceptable. Weaponizing food and endangering civilians and civil infrastructure is equally unacceptable. Food, food supply should never be allowed to be weaponized. Mining sea lanes also undermines supply lines of grains many vulnerable countries around the world depend on. And as we know, and it was already said, the sea lanes cannot easily be replaced through land routes. As a neighbor of Ukraine, we know this well. So it's high time to bring this attention, to bring this issue here to the UN, which affects all of us, not only countries near, but also far away. Hence, I am supporting the call for the moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea and ensuring that we have the freedom of navigation, ensuring that we have access countries and people, populations who have a dire need for those grains, which are right now in the storage facilities in Ukraine, have access to it. Thank you.
Thank you. And now I give the floor to Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkey, Beris Akinci. Please.

Since the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, we have endeavored to keep the Black Sea out of the conflict. Thanks to our meticulous implementation of the Montreal Convention and the launch of the Black Sea Grain Initiative, we succeeded in this goal until recently. However, in recent months, increasing attacks against civilian vessels in the Black Sea pose a serious threat in the region. We are particularly alarmed by the attacks targeting Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned vessels, including within Turkey's exclusive economic zone and search and rescue region. So far, at least 54 Turkish-owned, operated merchant vessels have been attacked. These attacks have resulted in the death of four Turkish citizens, while many more have been wounded. Such attacks are unacceptable, regardless of the motive behind them. The situation in the Black Sea also poses risks to global food security. It increasingly resembles the one that emerged following the outbreak of the war in 2022. Following the termination of the Black Sea Grain Initiative by Russia in July 2023, Turkey, together with the UN, focused on devising a new arrangement to ensure safety of commercial navigation. Although an understanding was reached between the sides in 2024, it fell through at the last minute, unfortunately. We cannot accept the current situation in the Black Sea as the new normal. The Black Sea Grain Initiative proved that diplomacy could indeed yield concrete results. Bridging the different views of the warring sides is certainly not an easy task. However, we spare no effort to achieve a breakthrough. Furthermore, we maintain our dialogue with the UN on this issue and hope that an agreement can be reached in the Black Sea as soon as possible. We believe that such an agreement would also give momentum to diplomatic efforts aimed at achieving lasting peace in Ukraine. Thank you.
Thank you. And now I give the floor to Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Environment and Culture of Liechtenstein, Sabine Monani.

Thank you for convening this meeting and thank you to today's briefers who have set out the challenges we face so eloquently. Liechtenstein, as always, stands with Ukraine and with its people. In the brief time I have today, I will focus on two aspects of the situation in the Black Sea: food security and maritime security. Russia's aggression against Ukraine is not only a full-scale attack on its independence, but also on the very symbols of its existence. Ukraine for so long has been the breadbasket of Europe, exemplified in its flag, showing a clear blue sky over golden fields of wheat. Yet today, around 25% of Ukraine's territory is suspected of contamination. And as it is well known, Russia has attempted to block the export of grain from Ukraine's Black Sea ports and continues to do so. We were pleased to see the UN leading on the Black Sea grain initiative, and we encourage both incumbent and incoming secretaries general to pursue exactly these kinds of peacemaking initiatives. The Russian Federation's actions in the Black Sea show how threats to maritime security can have far-reaching consequences for global food security. As a key route for the export of agricultural commodities, the Black Sea depends on the effective application of a common legal framework at sea. We recognize the role of UNCLOS in governing rights and obligations for all states at sea, as it reflects customary international law. Increasing sophistication and scale of Russia's shadow fleets are particularly concerning, undermining sanctions enforcement and maritime safety. Liechtenstein supports efforts to enhance maritime surveillance and enforcement to address these alarming developments. At a time when waterways around the world are at threat and hunger is increasingly weaponized, states must guarantee safer maritime corridors for the provision of essential commodities and uphold the maritime security rules that make such passages a reality. I thank you.
Thank you. And now I give the floor to Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands, Don Berendsen, please.

Thank you, Kaja, and thank you for all the co-hosts of this timely meeting. We've seen that in recent weeks, Russia has changed tactics. Attacks are now also on ports, ships, border crossings, civilian infrastructure, in broad daylight. And these attacks have severely disrupted Ukrainian exports. The Ukrainian economy, which depends heavily on farming and agri-food businesses, has been hit hard. And the impact goes far beyond Ukraine. Millions of families may face rising prices and hunger if the Russian attacks continue. And this tactic is deeply irresponsible. That's why the Netherlands supports the moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, being initiated by Ukraine and the European Commission. It should ensure that the food experts can reach global markets and the countries that depend on Ukrainian grain and other wheat products. At least three more measures are also crucial. Temporary storage of grain, working capital for farmers and small and medium-sized enterprises, and alternative export routes for grain and other products. And in this context, we also support the World Bank, World Food Programme, and the FAO. These organizations are working to install grain sleeves for storage and to provide capital to farmers and other businesses to help get them through the next season. And I urge EU member states to strengthen the solidarity lanes so that Ukraine can continue its food exports to global markets. The Netherlands will continue to stand by Ukraine, offering both military and non-military support, and together we will continue our commitment to Ukraine. We must remain united in confronting Russia's aggression and in safeguarding global food security. Thank you.
Thank you. Now I give the floor to Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom, Ed Miliband. Please, Ed.

Thank you. And can I thank you and French, Romanian, and Ukrainian partners for bringing us together on this crucial topic. And I will echo the words of many people who have already spoken around this table. This issue matters to the people of Ukraine, but it also matters to us all. It's about whether millions of people can put food on the table. and Russia's actions matter to every country represented in this room and indeed countries that are not here too. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, millions of people depended on food exported through Ukraine's Black Sea ports, and we know that the impact of the disruption is having far-reaching consequences. We also know, as others have said, where the blame lies. First, Russia tried to block Ukrainian exports, then it walked away from the Black Sea Grain Initiative. Now it is attacking grain exports, port infrastructure and civilian merchant vessels. And it is not just Ukrainians who are paying the price. It's important to say that seafarers, including from India and Egypt, have been killed. And the countries least able to absorb another shock are being hit the hardest. Ukraine has repeatedly offered a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire, and of course Russia has refused. So what can we do? This meeting is important. We have to respond together and speak with one voice in calling on Russia to stop these attacks and agree to the ceasefire that Ukraine has already offered. And as Tom has said just now, together we can also help limit the damage by keeping exports flowing, supporting alternative routes and protecting safe passage for commercial shipping. The UK is already working with partners to do exactly that. Royal Navy mine clearance experts are supporting efforts to keep Black Sea shipping routes safe and open. We stand shoulder to shoulder with the people of Ukraine on this and every other issue. We have shown before that international cooperation can keep Ukrainian grain reaching the people who need it most, and now is the time for renewed urgency and purpose to do so again. Thank you.
Thank you. And now I give the floor to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Czechia, Petr Machek, please.

Thank you, Kaja. And thank you for organizing this side event. Ladies and gentlemen, when we speak about the war in Ukraine, we often speak about front lines, about missiles, and about territory, etc. But today I think we speak about something much more ordinary. We speak about the price of bread. For millions of people far beyond Europe, the consequences of this war are not measured in kilometers from Kyiv or Odessa. They are measured in food prices and availability, and in uncertainty over whether supplies will reach those who need them. This reminds us one important fact. The Black Sea is not just a regional sea. It is one of the arteries of global trade. When ports, grain terminals or commercial vessels are attacked, the consequences do not stop at Ukraine's borders. They travel through global markets, and eventually reach households in Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and beyond. Ukraine is, of course, paying the highest price for this war, but it is not paying it alone.
